articles.title: American veterans targeted by schemes to steal benefits and exploit the sick, disabled: DOJ
articles.summary: The Justice Department launches a nationwide VA benefits fraud crackdown, charging 15 defendants in schemes with more than $3.4 million in intended losses.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX — Fraud schemes drained veterans’ disability benefits and left a promised cancer treatment center unfinished before it was demolished, according to the Justice Department. In launching a nationwide crackdown on abuse of veterans’ programs, the DOJ is levying charges against 15 defendants in schemes involving more than $3.4 million in intended losses, announcement materials obtained first by Fox News Digital detail. Prosecutors also secured guilty pleas, trial verdicts and sentencings in cases involving more than $19 million in intended losses during the operation, which began Sept. 1, 2026. DOJ’S ‘OPERATION GHOSTBUSTERS’ TARGETS MASSIVE STUDENT-AID FRAUD SCHEME BUILT ON FAKE ENROLLEES The operation marks the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division’s first coordinated nationwide surge focused on VA benefits, bringing together federal prosecutors, the Department of Veterans Affairs and its inspector general. "For veterans, benefits are not simply government payments," Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald said in a statement. "They are earned benefits -- earned through service, sacrifice, deployments, injuries, time away from loved ones, and a willingness to serve something larger than themselves." TEXAS CLINIC OWNER CONVICTED IN $26M MILITARY HEALTH FRAUD TIED TO GOLD-PLATED CYBERTRUCK Asked during Tuesday’s press conference whether uncovering $19 million in fraud represented a meaningful success given the scale of fraud nationwide, McDonald pointed to the veterans whose benefits and care were affected. "I would ask the question of the veterans who didn't get the care whether the $19 million that was stolen from them, whether it matters to them," McDonald said. "Whether the cancer center that was not built, did it matter to them that they did not have the cancer center that the taxpayer funded to be able to serve our warfighters and to seek to help them in their moment of need?" In Florida, the government paid approximately $4.8 million toward a veterans’ cancer treatment center that was never completed — and ultimately was demolished without being rebuilt, according to DOJ. The VA awarded the $8.9 million construction contract for the Cancer Infusion Therapy Center at Bay Pines VA Medical Center through a program reserved for businesses owned by service-disabled veterans. Evidence at trial showed that Matthew West, Kevin Kutina and their co-conspirators secured the contract while concealing arrangements under which ineligible companies would perform most of the work and receive most of the payments. West and Kutina were convicted of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud and major fraud against the United States. Two co-defendants pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Construction failures plagued the project, leaving the partially completed facility to be torn down, according to the DOJ. Other cases involved alleged theft directly from veterans’ benefit payments. In Texas, prosecutors allege that VA National Call Center employee Heidi Brady used her access to veterans’ personal information and knowledge of payment procedures to change their direct deposit details shortly before monthly disability payments were issued. The money allegedly went to an account she controlled. Her neighbor, Raymond Audie Davis, is accused of helping by impersonating veterans during calls to the VA and using their identifying information to redirect payments, according to the indictment. In Ohio, Darlene Toman allegedly stole from disabled veterans whose finances she was entrusted to manage — including a Marine severely wounded in Iraq who received the Purple Heart and Combat Action Ribbon. Prosecutors say the victims included people with traumatic brain injuries, schizophrenia, amputations and other serious conditions. Some required around-the-clock care. Rather than safeguard their benefits, Toman allegedly used fraudulent checks and diverted payments intended to cover veterans’ living expenses and care for her own use. The allegations against Brady, Davis and Toman have not been proven in court. Defendants are presumed innocent unless and until convicted. Fox News Digital's Stephen Sorace contributed to this report.

articles.title: Conservatives launch $10M anti-socialism blitz after Democrats dominate youth vote
articles.summary: YAF is launching a nationwide "Freedom Not Socialism" campaign in 30 Democratic strongholds after Democrats won the majority of the youth vote in the midterms.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: A conservative organization has launched a nationwide campaign of more than $10 million targeting at least 30 Democratic strongholds to combat the growing popularity of socialism among young Americans ahead of the 2028 presidential election. The Young America's Foundation (YAF), led by former Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker, announced its "Freedom Not Socialism" initiative, which will bring prominent conservative leaders, including possible 2028 contenders, scholars and activists, to schools and communities across the country to challenge the influence of democratic socialism among younger voters. "Our mission is to explain to people that their high cost of living is due to big government," Walker told Fox News Digital, explaining that the initiative will mobilize speakers to engage directly with young Americans at colleges, high schools and other institutions. SOCIALISM'S GROWING APPEAL MEETS AN AWKWARD REALITY CHECK ON COLLEGE CAMPUS The announcement comes after Democrats captured the majority of the youth vote in Tuesday's midterm elections. The group launched its first event in Santa Barbara, Calif., over the weekend. "YAF's initiative is vital for the future of our country because young Americans continue to get behind these false narratives of free this and free that, and they don't realize that the reason they are in the place where they cannot afford to live is because of big government," Rep.-elect Michael Alfonso, R-Wis., said. During his interview with Fox News Digital, Alfonso, the 26-year-old grandson of immigrants who escaped communist Cuba, argued that the American education system had failed the next generation by not teaching the history of socialist regimes. "The American education system has failed us," Alfonso said. "Young Americans do not know the truth about communist Cuba, communist Russia and communist Venezuela. All it takes is a simple look at these countries to realize how prosperous they were before communism came, and then what happened to them after." "If we started teaching kids real history in the schools, maybe we wouldn't have so many people that come out hating this nation," said the congressman-elect, who will become the youngest member of Congress. The group also announced plans to host a Freedom Conference in Dallas in early 2027 to prepare young conservatives to promote free-market principles and challenge socialist policies on college campuses. "Young Americans are going to be the majority of voters in 2028, and they are increasingly being sold the promises of socialism without understanding the devastating consequences that follow," Walker, YAF's president, told Fox News Digital. articles.title: US attorney threatens probe of Garcia over Trump investigation remarks
articles.summary: A U.S. attorney in Texas on Monday sent his fourth letter threatening to investigate a Democratic lawmaker, launching a “preliminary inquiry” into House Oversight and Government Reform Committee Chair Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) and telling him to preserve documents. Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, has no particular oversight into activities…
articles.body:
A U.S. attorney in Texas on Monday sent his fourth letter threatening to investigate a Democratic lawmaker, launching a “preliminary inquiry” into House Oversight and Government Reform Committee Chair Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) and telling him to preserve documents.

Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, has no particular oversight into activities that take place in Washington, D.C., or in the legislative branch.

But in a late Monday letter he accused Garcia of stretching the power of congressional oversight with his plans to investigate President Trump and those in his orbit.

“A committee’s gavel is not a prosecutor’s commission. Yet you cannot say that the investigations you fantasize about are confined to a lawful legislative end,” Reitz wrote.

Garcia’s team did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but he has defended his plans to investigate the administration as well as Trump’s family members and business dealings — arguing they are rooted in the legislative purpose Reitz says his investigations will need.

“Our work is about taking on government corruption, making life more affordable through bringing down costs by actually going after the crooks and the criminals that are causing harm, and then writing good legislation to stop the corruption from happening in the future,” Garcia said last week during an appearance on MS NOW.

“And so it’s outrageous that Donald Trump wants to stop any sort of oversight, and certainly he’s trying to stop us members of Congress from doing our job that is in the Constitution.”

Reitz last week sent a similar letter to Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), who is set to be the chair of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, and Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.).

Blumenthal, a former U.S. attorney, said last week that Reitz is the one edging toward a crime.

“I was absolutely astonished at the threats and bullying, which would have been ludicrous, but it was such a misuse of prosecutorial power. The threat to me is the absolute epitome of weaponization of the Department of Justice for political purposes,” he said.

“Interference in a congressional investigation is a violation of the Constitution by the executive branch. It’s a separate branch of government, and the Constitution insulates this type of investigation very explicitly from the kind of interference that he is threatening.”

Over the weekend, Reitz also wrote a letter to Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) — a lawmaker Trump has called “Pocahontas” — in which he confronted and accused her of being “on the warpath to wield her committee gavel like a tomahawk.” The letter goes on to reference smoke signals, and he describes the letter as his “first arrow shot.”

A column in Native News Online described the letter as using “insensitive references to Native American culture and history” that draw on “stereotypes that have portrayed Native Americans as violent, primitive or warlike.”

The crux of the letters from Reitz, as well as another sent by White House counsel Will Scharf, is that Democrats’ investigative efforts could be criminal in nature, particularly if they are brought to harass allies of the president. Democrats have said their probes are into legitimate malfeasance.

Joyce Vance, a former U.S. attorney appointed under former President Obama, wrote that Reitz’s efforts were “all hat, no jurisdiction.”

“Title 28 U.S.C. § 547 defines the responsibilities of United States Attorneys. They prosecute crimes. They defend the United States when it gets sued and bring affirmative civil lawsuits when appropriate. They collect money judgments on behalf of the United States. But each U.S. Attorney can only do that ‘within his district’ according to the statute,” she wrote in her blog.

“In a letter sent to Senator Warren, Reitz accuses her, along with Blumenthal and Garcia, of ‘demanding sweeping information’ from a private citizen—which is pretty much how investigations work. There’s no legitimate inference that the legislators are committing crimes; in fact, the suggestion in this context is ludicrous.”

Attorney General Todd Blanche implied last week he did not have advance knowledge of Reitz’s letter, saying, “I don’t oversee every single thing that’s done.”

But he also struck a less aggressive tone on dealing with congressional investigations.

“The Congress has an extremely important oversight function that allows them and actually requires them to do their jobs in conducting oversight. I have a job as the attorney general to protect the executive’s rights, also to be responsive in the right cases for oversight, which is what we’ve done the last year and a half, and that’s something that we’ll continue to do,” he said.

“I am optimistic, as is the president, that we will have a relationship with Congress that is productive.”

articles.title: ‘It’s life’: Trump brushes aside concerns about outages
articles.summary: President Donald Trump brushed off recent mass outages that wreaked havoc on air travel, banks and emails, saying Tuesday, “it’s life.”
articles.body: President Donald Trump brushed off recent mass outages that wreaked havoc on air travel, banks and emails, saying Tuesday, “it’s life.” “It’s life, it’s life,” he told reporters during his trip to the Philippines when asked about the outages. “When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.” Instances of mass outages in quick succession are rare. The recent outages affected Microsoft, air travel and Chase Bank and raised questions about technological vulnerabilities in widely used systems that have long been integrated into Americans’ daily lives. Last week, a nationwide ground stop apparently caused by a router issue ultimately led to thousands of canceled and delayed flights and left passengers stranded. Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare, and last week’s incident came shortly before the Thanksgiving travel period is set to kick off. Asked whether he was worried about Thanksgiving week travel, Trump said “not at all.” “People are safe,” he said. The succession of mass outages began Thursday, when more than a dozen Microsoft cloud services, including Outlook email and Teams messaging, went down. The outage snarled communications at businesses and schools across the country as people were unable to send or receive emails. A day later, the Federal Aviation Administration issued the rare ground stop for several hours after a system outage, which it said was caused by a router that overloaded older air traffic control equipment with data. On Monday, United Airlines faced another widespread system outage leading to more flight delays. That same day, Chase Bank faced a nationwide outage that stymied some customers from accessing their money. Trump affirmed to reporters that he has spoken with banks about the Chase outage. Asked what bank officials told him, Trump said, “It’s going to be very much under control.” He did not share further details about who he spoke with or the content of their discussion. Following Friday’s ground stop, neither Trump nor Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy took any blame for the situation. “I don’t take any responsibility,” Trump told reporters Monday as he left the White House for his Asia trip. Similarly, Duffy said in a Sunday interview on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that he “can’t apologize for what was passed off to us.” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin insisted in a CNBC interview Tuesday that the U.S. was not being attacked. “I can tell you with complete certainty that we are not under attack,” Mullin said. “There’s no cyber threat that’s taken place. The homeland is very secure.”

articles.title: Don’t sacrifice Minnesota’s Boundary Waters on the altar of permitting reform
articles.summary: Passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will make Congress members complicit in a massive intergenerational theft.
articles.body:
Americans across the country just delivered a stunning rebuke to President Trump and his party in the midterm elections. Democrats will now control both houses of Congress, with a clear mandate to chart a new path forward. Yet the first order of business for lawmakers this week is a bill that would codify the president’s pay-to-play vision for America’s public lands.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act threatens to sacrifice many beloved landscapes on the altar of permitting reform. For Minnesotans, the most cherished of these wild places is the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness, which is in imminent danger of being sold out to benefit a giant Chilean corporation. Passing the act would make this short-sighted national betrayal irreversible.

Like millions of Americans, I spent my formative years canoeing the serene lakes and flowing rivers of the Boundary Waters along the Canadian border. This vast 1.1-million-acre wilderness stretches across more than a thousand lakes . Its boreal forests are home to wolves, deer and moose, without a single trail sign imposing on nature’s design. Every year, around 150,000 people come to this magnificent place to cast a line for walleye, chart the night sky by the light of a campfire or hear the mournful call of a loon. It is the single most visited wilderness area in the country.

For more than 60 years, political leaders from both parties have wisely acted to protect the Boundary Waters from pollution and industrial development. Because of their commitment, every American today can freely share in the abundance that the Boundary Waters offers, free of charge. We are in desperate need of that wisdom now, as lawmakers consider abandoning that commitment to embrace a new political order, which prioritizes profits over people.

In 2015, Chilean mining giant Antofagasta acquired Twin Metals Minnesota and began planning an industrial copper-nickel mining complex next door to the Boundary Waters. It was able to do so after the first Trump administration made the decision to reinstate two expired federal mining leases.

The administration’s move was stopped and its leases cancelled by the Biden administration. But if the current administration gets its way , Antofagasta will soon have its mining leases again. Passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will mean that no future court and no federal agency can easily right the wrongs of the second Trump administration.

The bill’s “Project Certainty” makes it exceedingly difficult for any future administration to “revoke, rescind, withdraw, terminate, suspend, amend, or alter” these types of mining leases. That means a future administration could not cancel or withdraw Twin Metals’ leases — even if they are found to be unlawful. Even efforts to add more protective conditions to the leases for water pollution or wildlife conservation would likely be foreclosed.

The bill incentivizes government agencies to play along. While project proponents like Twin Metals could sue the government for damages, including paying for substantial portions of the project, courtroom access would be limited for the public, Tribal Nations, businesses and public interest organizations. Even if groups successfully sued, the act ties the courts’ hands by barring judges from vacating or enjoining leases that violate the nation’s bedrock environmental and cultural review laws.

What Antofagasta proposes to build in the headwaters of the Boundary Waters is not like the iron-ore mines, which are long-established in northern Minnesota. Copper-nickel mining produces sulfuric acid and heavy metals, with a consistent record of devastating environmental harm that includes contaminating waters, degrading forests and catastrophic spilling of highly toxic materials. It has never been done before in Minnesota.

Pollution from a Twin Metals mine — sulfate, sulfide and heavy metals — would permanently degrade the waters that flow through the heart of the Boundary Waters and reach further downstream to Voyageurs National Park, Quetico Provincial Park and Hudson Bay. In return for devastating northeastern Minnesota’s $1.1 billion outdoor tourism economy, Antofagasta will ship its metal concentrates abroad for processing and sale in China .

President Theodore Roosevelt, who in 1909, created the Superior National Forest that encompasses the Boundary Waters, called these public lands our “sacred heritage.” Even in today’s polarized political climate, Americans overwhelmingly share this view. Recent polling shows that 74 percent of Minnesotans support a permanent ban on copper-nickel mining in the Boundary Waters watershed.

Passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will make members of Congress complicit in a massive intergenerational theft. Where we once sought peace and solitude in the great outdoors, our children and grandchildren will be left with a toxic Chilean dumping ground. Lawmakers must stand strong in defense of the Boundary Waters — before it’s too late.

Mark Dayton served as a U.S. senator representing Minnesota from 2001-2007 and as the governor of Minnesota from 2011 to 2019.

articles.title: Bush-appointed judge torpedoes Trump immigration rule, rips DHS for overstepping its authority
articles.summary: A federal judge appointed by President George W. Bush ruled DHS overstepped its authority on the F-1 student visa, blocking fixed time limits.
articles.body: An immigration rule drafted by the Trump administration to plug an alleged gap in the visa system has met its end at the hands of a federal judge appointed by former President George W. Bush. District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV of Massachusetts ruled Monday that the Department of Homeland Security overstepped its authority by promulgating a rule that placed greater restrictions on visas for international students, exchange visitors and foreign journalists. His ruling represents a victory for the labor unions and university presidents that challenged the rule, and another loss in the Trump administration’s legal crusade to crack down on immigration. The DHS rule would have replaced a longstanding policy by only allowing international students to study in America for a fixed timeframe, generally capped at four years, requiring them to apply for an extension if they wish to continue their studies. Previously, there was no fixed time limit for international students so long as they remained enrolled in a university and otherwise maintained legal status. The rule also would have imposed new restrictions on transferring schools, changing academic programs and pursuing additional degrees, while subjecting students to additional immigration reviews intended to combat fraud and national security threats. TRUMP ADMIN SUED OVER VISA TIME RESTRICTIONS FOR FOREIGN STUDENTS, JOURNALISTS "DHS acknowledges that there are legitimate reasons why a student may pursue another academic degree at the same or lower level as the one he or she has completed — for example, pursuing an M.B.A. after a J.D.," the judge wrote. "But the Final Rule would effectively prohibit such a student from entering the United States to pursue those studies. And the purported reasons given by DHS for doing so — protecting national security and preventing fraud — are not reasonably related to the nature and purpose of the F-1 visa program." "Put bluntly, DHS is seeking to prevent or discourage the very activity — providing educational opportunities for foreign students in the United States — that Congress sought to permit and encourage," Saylor continued. "The statute simply does not grant DHS such broad and open-ended authority to undermine the F-1 visa program." US STATE DEPARTMENT HAS YANKED MORE THAN 175K VISAS UNDER TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SO FAR Saylor had already blocked the rule from taking effect in September, but Monday's ruling went further by striking it down entirely after finding that DHS violated federal administrative law. Lawyers representing the department disagreed with the judge’s characterization, arguing that indefinite admission periods prevent immigration officials from periodically reassessing whether foreign nationals are complying with the conditions of their visas. Mandatory extensions, in the telling of the agency, would create additional opportunities to identify fraud, security risks and immigration violations — risks it says are substantiated by past cases of fraud and abuse in the student visa system. "The performative outrage is incredible. Where was the outrage when foreign nationals were abusing the system, violating the terms of their student visas, and making a mockery of our immigration laws? If the media really cared about legitimate international students, they would be thanking President Trump for cracking down on the rampant fraud to ensure only those truly intending to study in the United States are given the privilege," a DHS spokesperson told Fox News Digital. Saylor, however, further argued that DHS failed to establish how its new rule would constitute an improvement over existing systems meant to catch visa fraud. "But DHS has not adequately explained how implementing an unreviewable, completely discretionary renewal system — after a foreign student has already been in the country for four years — meaningfully enhances the ability of DHS to root out cases of fraud, or how the benefits of such a system outweigh the immense costs of abandoning the existing system," he wrote. DHS PROPOSES MASSIVE $70K FEE FOR FOREIGN STUDENTS SEEKING WORK AUTHORIZATION Currently, DHS relies on the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) to monitor student visa fraud. SEVIS is a federal database that monitors international students and exchange visitors, tracking their enrollment, immigration status and compliance with visa requirements through information reported by schools and program sponsors. The agency argued that the system is a "data-reporting system for schools" that is "not designed for performing all relevant fraud and security screening." Saylor was identified as a Republican in a 2014 profile piece. The same piece noted Saylor had close ties to former Massachusetts Gov. Mitt Romney and that he was reportedly considered for a position in the Bush administration. He was confirmed by a bipartisan vote in the Senate, even winning the support of Democratic Sen. Ted Kennedy, a noted liberal, who praised him for his fair-mindedness and independence. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP DHS did not tell Fox News Digital whether it intended to appeal Saylor's ruling.

articles.title: For true picture of Nov. 3, look at the states
articles.summary: Democratic gains in the 2026 midterm elections across various state offices and legislatures have significantly shifted the balance of power and strengthened the potential for abolishing the Electoral College through the National Popular Vote Compact.
articles.body:
German statesman Otto von Bismarck is credited with being the first to observe that “politics is the art of the possible.” But, ironically, President Trump may deserve credit for proving it true — especially for Democrats.

After all, before the midterm elections of 2026, few would have thought it possible to elect the first openly-gay U.S. senator, Chris Pappas (D-N.H.); the first Muslim senator, Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.); the first Black senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction, Scott Colom (D); the first Native American woman senator, Democrat Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.); the first woman elected to the Senate from South Carolina , Annie Andrews (D); the first senator with spina bifida, Josh Turek (D-Iowa); and Julia Letlow (R), the first Republican woman elected senator from Louisiana .

But while most attention focuses on the lopsided shifts in power in the House and Senate, equally historic results occurred in races for governor. Again, especially, but not totally, for Democrats. Nov. 3 produced the first Black woman governor in American history, Keisha Lance Bottoms (D) of Georgia; America’s first Native American woman governor, Deb Haaland (D) of New Mexico; Gina Hinojosa (D), first Latina governor of Texas ; Xavier Becerra (D), first elected Latino governor of California ; the first female governors of Ohio, Minnesota, and Tennessee ( Amy Acton (D) Amy Klobuchar (D) and Marsha Blackburn (R), respectively) and the first Black governors of Nevada, Wisconsin, and Florida (Aaron Ford (D), David Crowley (D) and Byron Donalds (R), respectively).

Indeed, I would argue that, no matter how mind-blowing Democratic margins are in the House and Senate, their gains at the state level may prove to be more important and more lasting.

Before Nov. 3, Republicans held 26 governorships nationwide, to 24 for Democrats. Now that Democrats have flipped six governorships , they hold 30 to just 20 for Republicans.

Democrats also flipped 12 Republican-controlled legislative chambers — the most state chambers flipped in any election since 2010. They gained 364 state legislative seats and now hold 22 state government “trifectas,” where one party controls both the governor’s office and both legislative chambers.

It has been overused, but only the word “tsunami” can describe what a sea change that is. Starting January 2027, more than 75 percent of Americans will live in states governed by Democrats. From sea to shining sea, America is blue.

There are two big reasons those Democratic gains at the state level are so critical. One, because that’s where most of the action is. Over the last two years — when, out of deference to Trump, a Republican-controlled Congress basically shut itself down — the only opposition to Trump’s draconian policies on immigration, mass deportations, election security, Medicare, Medicaid, climate change and other issues came from state capitols, not from Washington. The need for governors to step up and resist harmful federal dictates will continue as long as Trump remains in office. And now there will be six more Democratic governors willing to do so.

The second big reason state-level Democratic victories are so important is that this puts America well within reach of eliminating the Electoral College. Getting rid of the antiquated, undemocratic Electoral College has long been a bipartisan goal. Over 1,000 resolutions have been introduced in Congress to get rid of it.

The effective abolition of the Electoral College does not, in fact, require a constitutional amendment — not if enough states sign the National Popular Vote Compact and agree to award all their electoral votes to the candidate who wins the national popular vote.

So far, 18 states and the District of Columbia have done so, for a total of 222 electoral votes — just 48 short of the 270 needed to elect a president . States with new Democratic governors — Nevada (6 electoral votes), Arizona (11), Michigan (15), Wisconsin (10), and Pennsylvania (19) — could provide 61 new votes, more than enough to assign the Electoral College to the dustbin of history.

Because of the Electoral College, five men have become president without winning the national popular vote — two of them, Trump and George W. Bush, in this century. Getting rid of the Electoral College and making sure that never happens again might be the biggest win of the midterms.

articles.title: Trump administration moves to restrict employer-sponsored green cards
articles.summary: The Department of Labor has proposed a rule that would update the standards for employer-sponsored green cards for foreign workers, in a move to tighten regulations and “enhance” protections for American workers. The proposed changes to the permanent labor certification program, also known as PERM, would require employers to expand their recruiting efforts for American…
articles.body:
The Department of Labor has proposed a rule that would update the standards for employer-sponsored green cards for foreign workers, in a move to tighten regulations and “enhance” protections for American workers.

The proposed changes to the permanent labor certification program, also known as PERM, would require employers to expand their recruiting efforts for American workers, according to a Monday press release from the Labor Department .

This includes requiring employers to “advertise positions for at least 90 calendar days and demonstrate that they made good-faith efforts to recruit qualified American workers.”

“American Workers are the best in the world, and they deserve the first and best job opportunities. Existing regulations have instead allowed companies to sponsor foreign workers without fully considering American workers first,” said Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling in the release.

“This proposed rule change will ensure American workers are first in line for high-skilled, high-paying job opportunities over foreign labor,” Sonderling added.

The proposed rule is open to public comment for 60 days.

It also aims to protect qualified American workers affected by layoffs by requiring “ongoing consideration of laid off workers” and stopping employers that have laid off American workers in the last two years from sponsoring foreign workers for similar positions, according to the Labor Department’s release.

Additionally, employers would also be restricted “from tailoring job opportunities to foreign workers.”

The announcement marks the latest move in the Trump administration’s crackdown on employer-based immigration.

Last month, tech giant Microsoft was suspended from the PERM program with Vice President Vance accusing the company of benefitting from PERM and the H-1B visa program while laying off thousands of American workers.

“There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more than Microsoft,” Vance said at a press conference.

Last year, the administration announced a $100,000 fee for H-1B visa application, a move blocked by a federal judge in June. In August, the Department of Homeland Security proposed a new rule that would charge $103,265 fee on H-1B visas for foreign workers.

articles.title: Vance vows US won’t make long-term commitment to Iran war
articles.summary: Vice President Vance on Monday vowed that the U.S. will not make a long-term commitment to the Iran war compared with past U.S. wars in the Middle East. Fox News host Laura Ingraham told Vance that he was being blamed for the memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Iran not being a success for…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance on Monday vowed that the U.S. will not make a long-term commitment to the Iran war compared with past U.S. wars in the Middle East.

Fox News host Laura Ingraham told Vance that he was being blamed for the memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Iran not being a success for Republicans before the 2026 midterm elections. Vance defended President Trump and said the president still has “a lot of options.”

“He ultimately decides to bring the conflict to a close,” Vance said. “He is not going to let this become a forever war, and the people who want it to become a forever war, they can attack me all they want to, because we signed up to not do this.”

The vice president elaborated that Trump campaigned on not starting new conflicts across the globe, though Trump later suggested the opposite . Trump decided to strike Iran because “he felt he had to destroy the nuclear program,” Vance said.

“But we are not going to allow this to become a 10- to 15-year commitment or, frankly, even a two-year commitment, despite the fact that a lot of neoconservatives and a lot of other people want us to stay there forever,” he said. “We’re not going to stay there forever.”

The vice president said he has “full confidence” Trump will resolve the conflict “with great results for the American people.”

The conflict was at a standstill for two months following multiple attempts to reach a ceasefire agreement.

This was until three recent attacks launched by the Islamic regime. The third of these attacks was on Tuesday, when Iran fired multiple one-way attack drones towards a U.S. radar facility in Bahrain. The drones were intercepted with no damage or injury to U.S. service members, according to U.S. Central Command.

Trump has signaled that he would not escalate the conflict after recent negotiations helped lower the steep price of gas, declaring the conflict “effectively over.” He dismissed reports that Iran is developing plans to deploy a “ dirty bomb ” on Washington.

“Well if there is, they will pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before,” Trump told reporters in Manila, Philippines, when asked about the plot.

Qatar led the push earlier this month for both sides to return to the negotiating table, with the backing of Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey. These talks appeared to have since stalled.

Iran has offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which it effectively closed off since the start of the conflict, as one of several conditions to end the conflict. Tehran has also requested that U.S. sanctions be lifted and that frozen assets be released, but the administration has rejected these conditions.

articles.title: Trump says US taking 'very seriously' any Iranian plot against Washington
articles.summary: Tehran rejects any suggestion it was plotting a so-called dirty bomb attack on the US capital as "baseless".
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has said the US is taking "very seriously" the potential for any Iranian plot to attack Washington DC, after he was asked about a CNN report citing US intelligence assessments.

In the Philippines, where he attended the Asean Summit, Trump nodded when asked by a journalist about the report that Tehran was planning to detonate a so-called dirty bomb in the US capital and said: "We're looking into it."

CNN cited unnamed US intelligence officials suggesting Iran could target senior figures in Trump's administration with such an attack.

Iran called the claim "baseless." Concerns about dirty bombs grew after the 9/11 attacks in 2001, although no such attack has ever occurred.

Such a device would contain radioactive material - such as uranium - which would be scattered through the air when its conventional explosive detonated.

The BBC has not independently verified CNN's reporting.

During his comments to reporters in Manila, Trump was asked whether there was reason to believe an attack was imminent.

"I hope it's not," he said, "but we take it very seriously because they [the Iranians] happen to be crazy."

In a statement before Trump's comments, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis wrote: "We remain vigilant monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland."

Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei rebutted the CNN article and other US reports.

He posted on X: "Those who initiated the aggression against Iran are now seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs by manufacturing and disseminating baseless allegations."

Imran Bayoumi, a geostrategy expert with the Atlantic Council in Washington DC and former policy adviser to the defence department, said that it remains "unclear how serious" would be the threat of a supposed Iranian dirty bomb.

"But Iran has planned and threatened to attack the US in the past," he said. "It is also unclear why this report is becoming public now."

articles.title: CAIR defends civil rights work against Trump’s ‘smear’
articles.summary: The US’s largest Muslim advocacy group urges President Trump to address rising hate crimes against Muslims.
articles.body:
The largest Muslim civil liberties organisation in the United States has condemned suggestions by President Donald Trump that it could face a blanket designation as a “terrorist” group.

The Council on American–Islamic Relations (CAIR) said the White House should be addressing violence against American Muslims, rather than attacking the rights group.

“The Trump administration should focus on addressing this surge in violent hate, not entertaining smears against the civil rights organisation that counters such hate,” CAIR said in a statement to Al Jazeera on Tuesday.

On Monday, Trump said he was considering giving a blanket “terrorist” designation to the Muslim Brotherhood and that his administration was also looking at CAIR, which is already classified as a “terrorist” group in Texas and Florida.

“CAIR is another one we are watching,” he said of the organisation.

When asked if he was considering naming CAIR as a foreign “terrorist” group, he responded: “I’m not going to say that yet, but it could happen.”

In its statement, CAIR said that it was “fully prepared to defend our civil rights work and the broader American Muslim community from any new attempts to censor free speech, punish dissent or otherwise undermine the rule of law”.

“Our advocacy for justice here and abroad is the real reason that anti-Muslim and anti-Palestinian extremists spend so much time obsessing over our work,” it said.

CAIR highlighted several recent violent attacks against the Muslim community across the US, saying, “anti-Muslim extremists have murdered three American Muslims at a mosque in San Diego, firebombed multiple mosques in Minnesota, [and] attempted to burn down one of the largest mosques in Alabama”.

Trump’s comments on Monday came during an exchange with reporters outside the White House, following a question about Egypt’s crackdown on the Muslim Brotherhood and whether Washington would consider a broader designation of the group.

Earlier this year, the Trump administration designated the Muslim Brotherhood chapters in Lebanon, Jordan and Egypt as foreign “terrorist” organisations.

Trump praised Egypt, where the Muslim Brotherhood originated, for cracking down on the group, indicating it did so at his urging.

“Egypt has clamped down very hard on the Muslim Brotherhood, at my request,” he told reporters as he left the White House on Monday.

articles.title: Mullin defends use of government plane to go to LSU-Texas game after ground stop
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday defended his use of a government plane to fly to the LSU-Texas college football gam...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday defended his use of a government plane to fly to the LSU-Texas college football game the day after a nationwide ground stop that caused massive travel disruptions and left people stranded across the country.

Mullin, speaking on CNBC, acknowledged earlier reporting in the New York Post that he flew to the game a day after all planes were grounded. Mullin's flight took place after the stoppage was lifted and as flights were back in the air. But thousands of flights were canceled because of the ground stop, and Mullin flew as people nationwide were forced to scramble for alternative travel options.

Mullin's flight comes as the ground stop is garnering increasing scrutiny, with Democrats in the Senate demanding that the Trump administration provide clear answers about what went wrong. The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it was pausing the installation of the routers that were linked to the ground stop.

Asked on CNBC whether he is required to fly on government planes and whether he paid for the trip personally, Mullin said yes.

"We would have never went if the airways weren't completely open," he said on CNBC. "They'd been completely open for 21 hours."

He added: "We would have never taken airspace if airspace wasn't open. And we still gotta live our lives at the same time."

Mullin took over as DHS secretary earlier this year from Kristi Noem , whose tenure was rocked by scandal over spending at the department, as well as an aggressive approach to immigration enforcement. Mullin vowed to serve as a steady hand for the department and keep it out of the headlines.

The Department of Homeland Security said Mullin was required by law to travel on a government plane. It said in a statement that he pays personally for any flight unrelated to government work.

"Secretary Mullin abides by all ethics requirements," it said.

The day before his flight, Mullin was at the White House alongside Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy giving updates on the ground stop.

The longest flight stoppage in 25 years lasted more than four hours and ended around 8:15 p.m. ET Friday, allowing some domestic flights to take off from U.S. airports. The stoppage resulted in thousands of canceled flights and massive disruptions at airports across the nation ahead of the busy Thanksgiving holiday.

President Donald Trump's administration has said the air traffic snarls were caused by a router issue in the aging air traffic control system. Trump on Monday got defensive during a lengthy — sometimes testy — exchange with reporters as he left the White House for his trip to Asia.

He faulted old technology and Democrats for the incident that caused upheaval at the country's airports — especially his predecessor, President Joe Biden.

"I don't take any responsibility" for Friday's ground stop, Trump said.

"What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack," the president said. He later noted: "Incredibly, everybody was safe. Nobody was hurt. No crashes, no nothing."

Trump was silent on the chaos until Sunday, when he posted on social media blasting his Democratic predecessor and asking Congress for more money to cover the cost of system improvements.

Catalini reported from Morrisville, Pennsylvania.

articles.title: Mamdani takes swipe at Trump administration's response to tech outages: 'Far from what many wanted to hear'
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Tuesday blasted the federal government's response to multiple technical outages that impacted Americans.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani took a swipe at the Trump administration Tuesday following days of tech outages sweeping the nation, saying that "the response that we heard from federal officials was far from what many wanted to hear." Mamdani spoke after the U.S. experienced a slew of technology disruptions that halted flights, email services and online banking platforms across the country. "What I will say to New Yorkers is both an understanding of their frustration, we are speaking about New Yorkers who had made plans for months, some of them years, about going on a trip with their family or coming home from a trip with their family. And frankly, the response that we heard from federal officials was far from what many wanted to hear," Mamdani said. "And it did not leave many New Yorkers with any greater sense of confidence about our national capabilities in case of this occurring again," he continued. "And I'm looking forward to seeing Democratic majorities in the House and the Senate utilize that power to also ensure that we're delivering more answers at a national level, because what we were hearing from some of the secretaries that day was in no way confidence building." DUFFY VOWS TO MODERNIZE AGING AIR TRAFFIC SYSTEM AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House for comment. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said two routers from Federal Aviation Administration facilities in Texas and Arkansas are undergoing extensive testing as investigators examine whether faulty equipment or an installation problem triggered the nation's longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years this past Friday. The shutdown occurred as contractor L3Harris was replacing aging copper wiring with fiber-optic technology in the FAA's communications system. Duffy then said during an appearance on Fox News' "Hannity" Monday that he plans to modernize America’s aging air traffic control system and build new architecture that is "worthy of America." The secretary also said intelligence agencies found no evidence of a cyberattack. DHS CHIEF TELLS AMERICANS TO 'BREATHE' AMID TECH OUTAGES, INSISTS HOMELAND IS 'SECURE' The roughly five-hour ground stop affected more than 1.5 million passengers whose flights were scheduled to depart on Friday afternoon and evening. More than 12,000 flights were canceled that day, according to the FAA, while delays and cancellations continued through the weekend. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin also said Monday on "Hannity" that "the homeland is secure. "Our banking system is secure and when something like this happens, we’re able to react and react fast," Mullin continued. Mullin’s remarks came as customers Monday reported trouble accessing online services of major U.S. banking platforms, including Wells Fargo, Chase, U.S. Bank and Bank of America. United Airlines also faced a widespread system outage on Monday that briefly affected departing flights. Fox News Digital's Nora Moriarty, Stephen Sorace and Landon Mion contributed to this report.

articles.title: Sherrill commits $20.2M to deportation defense while condemning Rutgers over Border Patrol speaker
articles.summary: Mikie Sherrill condemned Rutgers College Republicans over a Gregory Bovino event while pouring $20.2 million into New Jersey's deportation defense program.
articles.body: New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill put her money where her mouth was this week as the Democrat criticized Rutgers University’s College Republican chapter for hosting a top former Border Patrol leader around the same time her administration allocated millions to a program meant to help illegal immigrants and others in the state fight deportation. Sherrill’s condemnation of the Rutgers students’ event drew criticism on X from observers who said it fueled protests outside the New Brunswick building where retired Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino spoke. Protests erupted inside the room as well, with video from inside showing Bovino responding to shouting protesters before he was briefly led out of the forum. "Everyone in this country is entitled to due process and a fair hearing under the law — regardless of where they were born," Sherrill said Friday in announcing a total of $20.2 million to fund the Detention Deportation Defense Initiative within Trenton’s Office of New Americans. NJ TAXPAYERS ON THE HOOK FOR $12M MORE AS DEM GOVERNOR PROTECTS ILLEGAL ALIENS BATTLING DEPORTATION Some of the funds will help migrants held at Delaney Hall in Essex County, where nightly protests have erupted since May. The governor previously visited the facility in solidarity with the detainees inside, while Sherrill ally Sen. Andy Kim, D-N. J., drew widespread attention online after being caught in a cloud of pepper spray dispersed by ICE toward surrounding protesters. "With the Trump Administration ramping up ICE activity and creating impossible obstacles for people facing detention and deportation to navigate alone, New Jersey is stepping up to connect residents with qualified legal counsel and equip more attorneys to take on this vital work," Sherrill said Friday, adding that the state’s immigrant community should not have to face a "complex" legal system alone. Commissioner Stephen Cha, head of Sherrill’s Department of Human Services, where the Office of New Americans sits, added in a statement that access to legal representation upholds due process and promotes a more "efficient" immigration system. The $20.2 million will be spread among 10 service providers and continue the Murphy-era initiative’s mission to offer legal expertise and representation for "low-income residents facing detention and deportation." EXCLUSIVE VIDEO: DEMS SLAMMED FOR DEMANDING ‘FIVE-STAR ACCOMMODATIONS’ FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS AT ICE FACILITY Sherrill’s new cash infusion nearly tripled the initiative’s most recent budget allocation. After Sherrill announced plans in June to increase the deportation defense initiative’s funding, Republicans in the state warned that the money could be better spent elsewhere, including on New Jersey residents. "New Jersey families are being crushed by some of the highest electric bills, property taxes, and costs of living in the entire country, and Governor Sherrill's answer is to spend more than $20 million defending illegal immigrants," said outgoing Rep. Jeff Van Drew, R-N.J., who was unseated by Cape May Mayor Zachary Mullock in this month’s blue wave. "It is a complete insult to every hardworking taxpayer in this state. New Jersey citizens should come first. If they can find $20 million for immigration lawyers, they can find money to lower utility delivery charges or provide relief to the people who actually live, work and pay taxes here." Van Drew said in June that every dollar Trenton spends on an illegal immigrant is a dollar that could have helped keep a New Jersey family from leaving the state. A DHS spokesperson said Sherrill has "consistently shown more concern for criminal illegal aliens who've broken our laws and destroyed any possibility of ever remaining in our country than she ever has for Rachel Morin, Laken Riley, Jocelyn Nungaray and the true victims of illegal alien crimes in America," while adding it does not comment specifically on matters involving former personnel like Bovino. Fox News Digital reached out to Sherrill for comment. Sherrill had publicly condemned Bovino and Rutgers’ College Republicans for holding the event. Rutgers is New Jersey’s state university, and the governor appoints some of its board members. Delaware Valley radio host Rich Zeoli said the state gives the New Brunswick school about $1.4 billion annually, adding the argument can be made she is "using a classic intimidation tactic to silence speech she doesn't like." MARKWAYNE MULLIN GOES OFF ON DEMS’ 'GARBAGE' MEMORIAL DAY ‘POLITICAL STUNT’ AT ICE FACILITY Sherrill urged attendees to press Bovino on why he chooses "cruelty over humanity" and what he thinks of the November election results and the argument that they represent a collective rebuke of his enforcement approach. The North Carolina native shot back at Sherrill, saying her statement was "spoken like a true lib who puts illegal aliens before her own citizens." "Gubner, I am deeply disappointed in your penchant for using the Governor’s Office to limit Constitutional rights of Americans," Bovino said in a statement. "This coming from someone who cheated at the Naval Academy (you weren’t allowed to walk), and enriched yourself via insider trading in defense stocks as a Congressgirl — priceless." Sherrill has said she was barred from walking at the graduation not because she was involved in cheating but because she declined to identify classmates involved. New Jersey State Assemblyman Paul Kanitra, R-Point Pleasant Beach, said Sherrill’s criticism of Bovino contrasts with her silence over Democrats electing a candidate in the state who was once acquaintances with the mastermind behind the 1993 World Trade Center bombing. "The thought-police strike again," Kanitra said. "I didn’t see you weighing in when any Adam Hamawy said some pretty heinous things recently? That didn’t seem to warrant a tweet," he said, referring to the Mercer County doctor and former defense trial witness for the Blind Sheikh who won the race to succeed retiring Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, D-N.J. Hamawy was never charged with any wrongdoing in connection with Abdel-Rahman, and his campaign previously told Fox News Digital related criticisms amount to "guilt-by-association" shaming and that Republicans and right-wing press are simply concerned that Hamawy will be "Donald Trump's worst nightmare." Bovino later challenged Sherrill to attend his event, which the governor did not attend. articles.title: Judge to order release of some records in federal search of Ilhan Omar’s home
articles.summary: A federal judge said Tuesday that he agreed with the Justice Department that the “vast majority” of the search warrant affidavit connected to an investigation of Rep.
articles.body: A federal judge said Tuesday that he agreed with the Justice Department that the “vast majority” of the search warrant affidavit connected to an investigation of Rep. Ilhan Omar should remain sealed. But Chief Judge James E. Boasberg said he believes that a back-and-forth between attorneys and a federal magistrate judge about measures to protect the lawmaker’s “speech and debate” rights should be released. “I agree that the vast majority of the warrant affidavit should remain sealed,” Boasberg said at a court hearing Tuesday, adding that it was “premature” to unseal the whole search warrant affidavit. He later added that he believed material should be unsealed about the “speech and debate” rights of Omar. “All of the legal debate about speech and debate, I don’t believe that should be redacted,” Boasberg said. The speech and debate clause of the Constitution is designed to protect the independence of the legislative branch, and states that federal lawmakers “shall not be questioned in any other Place” about their speech. Omar’s D.C home was searched in early October, an unusual overt investigative act against a sitting member of Congress within just weeks of the election. As NBC News reported, Omar’s phone was seized as part of the search. The search was authorized by federal Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh, who put protocols in place to protect Omar’s rights as a member of Congress, but those protocols were not made public. Omar, who won reelection earlier this month, said after the search that it was “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” saying Trump had targeted her for 10 years with “baseless lies and smear campaigns.” NBCUniversal News Group is part of a media coalition seeking access to the sealed search warrants connected to the Omar investigation. Alessandra Serano, a Justice Department attorney who works in the office of the deputy attorney general, acknowledged during the hearing that they were still reviewing materials seized from Omar’s home. “Why can’t a bunch of this be unsealed now?” Boasberg asked Serano. “I’m not talking about the warrant affidavit, but the litigation that takes place on the docket, I’ve gone though all of those documents and there are very few that say anything about investigative facts or identify witnesses … Why can’t those be unsealed now?” Serano said that there was material that could be unsealed about the discussion of speech and debate. “None of that, you would agree, requires the mention of any witnesses, of the government’s potential charges, of the government’s evidence it has developed, right?” Boasberg asked. But the Justice Department sought to keep the nature of the potential charges against Omar sealed. People familiar with the investigation have told news outlets including NBC News that it revolves around potential immigration-related crimes. Omar is a naturalized United States citizen who came to America as a child. Boasberg pointed out that Vice President JD Vance and President Donald Trump had spoken publicly about the investigation, and even acknowledged the specific type of investigation. Vance said earlier this year that he believed Omar “definitely committed immigration fraud” and specified after the search that it related to immigration fraud. “We’ve got your superiors saying what the government is looking into,” Boasberg said. “I had zero control over what was said,” Serano said. “That seems to be a common refrain,” Boasberg said with a laugh.

articles.title: Veteran pilot: Congress must act to update 'archaic' FAA tech that is 'putting Americans in danger'
articles.summary: Retired Air Force pilot Buzz Patterson warns the FAA ground stop will happen again, blaming "tribal" politics for delaying a $50 billion modernization.
articles.body: Friday's historic FAA ground stop will not be the last, a retired Air Force veteran and commercial pilot warns, unless Congress takes action and provides funds for the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to update what he calls a "broken" and "archaic" system that is "putting Americans in danger." "It's time for both parties to step up and say our AT system is degraded, it's old," retired Lt. Col. Buzz Patterson, who carried the nuclear football for former President Bill Clinton and is a retired 16-year Delta Air Lines pilot, told Fox News Digital in an interview this week. "We're putting Americans in danger when they get into an airplane, and we're putting the air crews in danger when they get into an airplane, if we continue to fly under archaic system, and that's what we're doing right now, it's archaic." FORMER TOP FAA OFFICIAL WARNS OF 48-HOUR RECOVERY AFTER AGING TECH 'OVERWHELMED' AHEAD OF GROUND STOP Too many administrations from both parties have "kicked the can" down the road on the complex and pricy overhaul, according to Patterson. "We've dug a big hole here, and we're trying to dig out of it," he said. "It's not going to take place overnight. It's going to be a long, grinding, devoted effort, and I think it's time for our politicians to get on board and fix it." TRUMP'S $50B AIR TRAFFIC CONTROL OVERHAUL FACES GOP PUSHBACK AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP Patterson, who just moved to Nevada and bought a new home he is renovating, said the $50 billion cost now laid bare by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy this weekend is akin to buying a home and immediately renovating it: Double down for the long-term benefits, if not savings. "Our technology, I mean, we're still using floppy disks, for God's sakes, in some of our facilities," Patterson lamented. "Last time I was in a tower, they were still using paper scripts to show what airplanes were supposed to taxi next. This should all be automated ... I mean, this should be easy-peasy, and we've made it so difficult." "We have way, way too much traffic to have an antiquated 1970s technology trying to drive our airplanes around the skies," he added, noting he "can't tell you the number of traffic avoidance calls I've gotten from ATC over the years that if I had not heard them, I probably would have hit somebody, or they would have hit me: so, it's essential." Patterson, who now flies frequently as a commercial passenger himself, stressed that aviation safety transcends party lines and urged Washington to abandon what he called "tribal" politics to pass comprehensive modernization funding. "It should be bipartisan, because I think if only one party pushes it, tries to push it through, it's not going to have success," he said. "I don't care what your political affiliation is: If you want to fly safely in our country, regardless of where you're going, or who you are, then you should be able to. And right now I think it's become tribal, where Democrats don't want to do anything that supports Trump or the FAA, and Trump's trying to get some stuff done." BUTTIGIEG TAKES SWIPE AT TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AMID FAA FLIGHT CHAOS Even President Donald Trump is "late" to conduct the overdue modernization, but he is also facing congressional gridlock, too, Patterson lamented. "He's late, granted, he's late, but every other president's been late too – and so Duffy asking for $50 billion, I understand that is probably too little, too late, but it's a start." While praising the dedication of current air traffic controllers and flight crews, Patterson warned that human skill can only compensate for technological limitations for so long. He noted that pilots still rely heavily on traditional voice radio relays rather than seamless, automated cockpit-to-ground data and weather integration, recalling numerous midair traffic avoidance calls from controllers over his career that prevented potential collisions. BUTTIGIEG TRASHES DUFFY’S GROUND STOP RESPONSE, BUT HIS DOT FAILURES DOOM HIS 2028 BID Patterson said weather radar, FAA and ATC can all be upgraded to improve airline safety, noting the recent Learjet 60 crash in Florida. "You don't fly through that stuff, you just don't," Patterson said of the Learjet 60 crash that featured pilots seeking a direct route through a thunderstorm. "If you do, you're going realize why you don't, because it's going to bang the crap out of you if you get through it. And in this, in this case, they didn't get through it." FLORIDA PLANE CRASH INVESTIGATORS SAY WEATHER CONDITIONS A 'MAJOR FOCUS,' PLANE MAY HAVE STARTED TO BREAK UP Communications, weather radar, routers and copper to fiber optic wiring upgrades all go hand-in-hand for safety, according to Patterson. "There is an interconnectivity between the National Weather Service and the FAA," he said. "There's an interconnectivity there that could be had if we upgrade our ATC capabilities, and we can somehow connect. "And it shouldn't be too hard to connect the National Weather Service directly to the cockpit, and I think that's where we're going to have to go, and I think that's necessary. And it's also not ironic that the same day ATC went down, the National Weather Service went down. I'm not saying it was a coordinated activity. I'm just saying that is the basis of our aviation system. "And if we don't have the most advanced air traffic control technology and the most advanced weather technology, then we, as the world's superpower, we have failed dramatically, and I think that's where we are." DUFFY: INVESTIGATORS EXAMINING 2 ROUTERS AFTER NATIONWIDE FAA GROUND STOP, NO SIGNS OF FOREIGN CYBERATTACK With peak holiday travel approaching, Patterson warned that systemic meltdowns will continue to disrupt the flying public until Washington commits to a sustained, multiyear overhaul. "I'm going to say this won't be the last one; it's going happen again," Patterson said of the nationwide ground stop. "It's probably going happen on Thanksgiving Eve or Christmas Eve, and people are going to wonder why it's happening, and I'm going tell you why it's happening: It's because our infrastructure is broken, and our ATC needs help, and the FAA needs help." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I think Sean Duffy is doing a phenomenal job," he concluded. "He's done more as a DOT guy than anybody that I can possibly remember since I started flying, and I think that what we're seeing right now is decades of neglect on the part of both parties. I mean, I'm not going to absolve Republicans either, because I'm looking at this as a pilot and as an American with a family, and I want to be able to fly my family safely around the country, and I don't feel safe putting my family on an airplane right now until we figure this out."

articles.title: Jeffries endorses lowering Medicare age, adding benefits and universal coverage for kids
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N
articles.body: WASHINGTON — House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is calling for an aggressive health care agenda next year for the new Democratic majorities in Congress. Jeffries, who is the heavy favorite to become speaker of the House on Jan. 3, said Democrats should use their “historic” House majority and “robust” Senate majority to lower the Medicare eligibility age and expand coverage under the program to include benefits for dental, vision and hearing. He also backed universal health coverage for children. “We should lower the age of Medicare eligibility. We should expand coverage to include vision, hearing, and dental. And we should cover all the kids in the United States of America,” Jeffries said Tuesday in response to a question from NBC News. “Those are bold actions, meaningful actions, important actions that can be taken on our march toward universal health coverage.” The remarks by Jeffries go significantly further than the pre-election health care agenda he laid out in September, which focused on undoing President Donald Trump’s Medicaid spending cuts and restoring enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits that expired in January. The Democratic leader reiterated his call for those policies on Tuesday, in addition to funding medical research for pediatric cancer, among other areas. He said Congress must go further, though he didn’t say what age to set Medicare eligibility at. “Right out of the gate, we will aggressively work on fixing the extraordinary damage that’s been done,” he said. “But we also know, as Democrats, that a return to the status quo is not acceptable. ... As part of our commitment that goes all the way back to FDR and Harry Truman to achieving universal access to health care for the American people.” Jeffries kept the door open when asked if he favors advancing health care measures in a filibuster-proof “reconciliation” bill that can bypass the Senate’s 60-vote threshold and pass without any Republican support. That would make such a bill more likely to land on Trump’s desk, forcing him to decide whether to sign it into law. Democrats are currently on pace to end up with 259 House seats and 56 Senate seats (with Alaska likely to be won by Democrats), according to NBC News estimates and projections. “Given the majorities that we’ll have in the House and the Senate, our two respective caucuses are going to have to work their will in conversation with each other,” Jeffries said. Among other key committee chairs who would be involved in negotiating such a bill, Jeffries mentioned “Bernie Sanders, the OG from Brooklyn,” who will chair the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. Sen. Sanders, I-Vt., the leading champion of Medicare for All, said that Jeffries appears to be “essentially supporting the first year” of his Medicare for All proposal, which he said includes a Medicare eligibility age of 55, plus extending benefits and covering all children. “Medicare for All is a four-year transition program,” Sanders said, adding that the Jeffries’ approach would represent good progress.

WASHINGTON — House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is calling for an aggressive health care agenda next year for the new Democratic majorities in Congress.

Jeffries, who is the heavy favorite to become speaker of the House on Jan. 3, said Democrats should use their "historic" House majority and "robust" Senate majority to lower the Medicare eligibility age and expand coverage under the program to include benefits for dental, vision and hearing.

He also backed universal health coverage for children.

"We should lower the age of Medicare eligibility. We should expand coverage to include vision, hearing, and dental. And we should cover all the kids in the United States of America," Jeffries said Tuesday in response to a question from NBC News. "Those are bold actions, meaningful actions, important actions that can be taken on our march toward universal health coverage."

The remarks by Jeffries go significantly further than the pre-election health care agenda he laid out in September , which focused on undoing President Donald Trump's Medicaid spending cuts and restoring enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits that expired in January .

The Democratic leader reiterated his call for those policies on Tuesday, in addition to funding medical research for pediatric cancer, among other areas. He said Congress must go further, though he didn't say what age to set Medicare eligibility at.

"Right out of the gate, we will aggressively work on fixing the extraordinary damage that's been done," he said. "But we also know, as Democrats, that a return to the status quo is not acceptable. ... As part of our commitment that goes all the way back to FDR and Harry Truman to achieving universal access to health care for the American people."

Jeffries kept the door open when asked if he favors advancing health care measures in a filibuster-proof "reconciliation" bill that can bypass the Senate's 60-vote threshold and pass without any Republican support. That would make such a bill more likely to land on Trump's desk, forcing him to decide whether to sign it into law.

Democrats are currently on pace to end up with 259 House seats and 56 Senate seats (with Alaska likely to be won by Democrats), according to NBC News estimates and projections.

"Given the majorities that we'll have in the House and the Senate, our two respective caucuses are going to have to work their will in conversation with each other," Jeffries said.

Among other key committee chairs who would be involved in negotiating such a bill, Jeffries mentioned "Bernie Sanders, the OG from Brooklyn," who will chair the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee.

Sen. Sanders, I-Vt., the leading champion of Medicare for All, said that Jeffries appears to be "essentially supporting the first year" of his Medicare for All proposal, which he said includes a Medicare eligibility age of 55, plus extending benefits and covering all children.

"Medicare for All is a four-year transition program," Sanders said, adding that the Jeffries' approach would represent good progress.

articles.title: ‘It’s fine’: Trump appears bent on proving he’s out of touch after 2026 losses
articles.summary: One of the biggest takeaways from Democrats’ historic 2026 rout was that voters saw President Donald Trump as out of touch. He seems bent on proving they wer...
articles.body:
One of the biggest takeaways from Democrats' historic rout in the 2026 midterm elections was that voters saw President Donald Trump as out of touch and uninterested in their plights.

The CNN Voter Poll showed 63% of voters said Trump prioritized his personal interests over the country's interests. And 64% said Trump did not "fight for people like you."

The president has spent the two weeks since the election doing the opposite of course correcting. Indeed, he seems bent on proving that voters were right.

Over the past 14 days, Trump has doubled down on his dismissal of Americans' economic problems, shrugged off a series of major systemic and governmental failures, and gone right on focusing like a laser on his gilded renovations of Washington and the White House.

The most striking comment came early Tuesday when Trump landed in the Philippines.

Asked about a series of recent events that have rocked Americans' everyday lives — a full ground stop at airports and outages and software problems from Microsoft, Chase Bank and United Airlines — Trump effectively turned himself into the "This is fine" meme .

"It's life," Trump said. "When you're big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen. It's fine."

The response exemplified the metaphorical shrug Trump has offered in recent days about the FAA ground stop and the growing Nvidia scandal.

After it was reported that then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman who is suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence — and whose company is suspected of illicitly funneling AI chips to China — Trump repeatedly downplayed the story.

He's also cast doubt on the idea that Alice Huang was a spy. (The US intelligence community is still working to understand the relationship between the Chinese businesswoman and the Chinese government.)

And Trump responded to a remarkable spat between two of his Cabinet secretaries by suggesting it was a simple philosophical disagreement about confronting China.

He also downplayed the severity of the potential Chinese espionage, saying, "China plays games with us, and we play games with China."

Just to underscore — as CNN's Stephen Collinson does — this isn't just a sex or even a corporate scandal. This is about whether the leading US adversary compromised the most valuable company in the United States, which is vital to winning the AI race against China. (China has denied the reports.)

And it's also a scandal that has cost many Americans a significant amount of money, thanks to the tumbling Nvidia stock.

Trump's response to the ground stop has been similar.

Despite it snarling travel throughout the weekend and leaving travelers apoplectic, Trump said next to nothing about the ground stop for two days. And even when he finally weighed in on Sunday, he merely issued some perfunctory-sounding social media posts asking Congress for more money.

Speaking of money, Trump has done almost nothing to change his dismissive posture toward Americans' economic concerns that cost the GOP so dearly.

In a social media post on Monday, he again claimed that the economy was " booming! " This is despite the Voter Poll showing just 2% of voters in the midterms saying the economy was "excellent" and three-quarters saying it was "not so good" or "poor."

(Trump spent more than a year telling people that they were wrong and that the economy was, in fact, in a new golden age, but they clearly didn't feel it .)

At the same time, Trump has downplayed his own wealth growth over the last two years (largely thanks to his ethically dubious cryptocurrency venture) by claiming in a "60 Minutes" interview after the election that "everyone" has done well and pointing to the stock market.

Except many Americans don't hold substantial amounts of stock, and wage growth hasn't kept pace with inflation for most of 2026. The CNN Voter Poll showed just 17% of voters said their families' financial situation was better than two years ago.

And finally, there's Trump's continued focus on his renovations in Washington — things like the White House ballroom, his proposed triumphal arch and overhaul of the golf course in East Potomac Park.

When challenged Monday on whether he was too focused on such things, Trump became angry, insisting he spends only "10 minutes a day" on the subject and that it "doesn't cost money."

But it's clearly a priority for him. The ballroom was Trump's first public event after his party's drubbing two weeks ago (after a stop at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool the day before the election). He's fighting legal battles so he can build the arch and renovate the golf course. On Saturday he posted more than half a dozen times with images of East Potomac Park , suggesting it was in disrepair. And on Monday, he posted images of gold statues .

In other words, he seems rather preoccupied.

"It was sort of mentioned a little bit during the campaign about, 'Why does Trump spend time on the White House?'" Trump said during his ballroom visit the day after the election. "Well, first of all, it's very little time. Second of all, I like it, it's good. For me it's relaxing. … I love construction."

Here is Trump doing a lot of the things he was doing before the election and that polls suggested were probably hurting him and the GOP.

A July CNN poll showed 73% of Americans said that Trump was not in touch with the problems that Americans face. A September CNN poll showed 74% said Trump hadn't paid enough attention to the country's most important problems.

And pre-election AP-NORC polling showed just 23% said Trump prioritized the country "a lot" and 11% said he prioritized "people like me" that much — compared to majorities who said he prioritized his and his friends' and family's business interests "a lot."

While before the election Trump and those around them could delude themselves into believing that maybe his bizarre political strategies and focus on unpopular policies didn't matter that much, the 2026 election results should have disabused anybody of those notions.

But recognizing the problem is only a small part of resolving it. The other part is getting a stubborn 80-year-old man whose aides appear allergic to questioning him to change his stripes.

And Trump seems to have no interest in that.
