articles.title: Classified NSA network went down, but no indication it was an attack, sources say
articles.summary: A classified computer network used by the National Security Agency went down due to a technical problem Tuesday, but there was no indication that it was an attack, sources say
articles.body: WASHINGTON — A classified computer network used by the National Security Agency went down due to a technical problem Tuesday, but there was no indication that it was caused by an attack, according to two people with knowledge of the matter and a senior U.S. cybersecurity official. The NSA’s network issue came amid mass outages that have wreaked havoc on air travel, banks and emails over the past few days. Though such mass outages in quick succession are rare, U.S. officials say there is no sign that the technical problems were caused by a coordinated cyberattack. President Donald Trump, when asked about the outages during his trip to the Philippines, said: “It’s life, it’s life. When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.” The NSA outage happened during maintenance on the network, the sources said. There was no sign that the outage affected the work of the NSA, which oversees America’s vast electronic surveillance efforts. It is not uncommon for government networks to suffer from brief disruptions or outages. CNN first reported on the network going down. A U.S. official said in a statement that “the National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.” The official added: “While some internal systems were affected, mission/critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend National Security continues.” Emily Harding, a former CIA analyst now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank, said that government systems “are highly redundant, so an outage like this won’t stop the work of national security.” “Government systems generally are outdated and in need of repair. This is another wake-up call to invest in better systems,” she said. The NSA incident came after a series of online outages and disruptions in recent days affecting Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration’s systems, JPMorgan Chase and United Airlines. The widely used online systems have long been a part of Americans’ daily lives. The outages have raised questions about technological vulnerabilities. James Lewis, a former senior government official and cybersecurity expert, said it was “a little unusual” for the NSA to have this kind of problem. “But across the government, it’s fairly common.” “It’s because the software is so complicated; it’s not always up to date,” he said. “When people try to patch it, they break it. So, it probably happens a lot more than we hear because it’s agencies that people don’t have as much interest in. But for NSA, it’s unusual. They probably weren’t affected by it, but it’s not that unusual to have systems crash.” Tom Winter reported from New York. Dan De Luce, Gordon Lubold and Julie Tsirkin reported from Washington.

articles.title: Jeffries shifts strategy amid growing Democratic divisions in US House
articles.summary: The lawmaker is opting to put progressive opponents on record as he vies to become the chamber’s first Black speaker.
articles.body:
On the eve of Democratic leadership elections in the United States House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries has confirmed plans to force fellow Democrats to take a recorded vote on his nomination for speaker.

Jeffries, the chamber’s current minority leader, told reporters at the US Capitol on Tuesday he was taking the new approach instead of — as some of his top allies had hoped — a vote by acclamation, which requires no ballot.

The move effectively forces House Democrats to publicly weigh in on whether they support Jeffries’s leadership.

Jeffries, a New York Democrat poised to become the House’s first Black speaker, argued that a recorded vote was the same method his party used when it retook control of the chamber in 2018 during President Donald Trump’s first term.

“It certainly seems to me to be appropriate that we take exactly the same approach to give every single person the opportunity to weigh in, one way or the other, on who the caucus feels is best positioned … to help move us forward into the new Congress,” Jeffries said during his news conference.

The strategy shift, which was first reported by Punchbowl News, comes amid growing Democratic dissent over having Jeffries in control of the party’s messaging and policy priorities in the US House.

Some progressive members, particularly newly elected ones, had reportedly threatened to call for a recorded vote to extract policy concessions from Jeffries.

Without unanimous backing, the vote to nominate Jeffries could highlight dissent within the Democratic Party.

One of the most vocal holdouts, Congressman-elect Don Leonard of Ohio, has publicly refused to commit to Jeffries unless he received guarantees on some progressive priorities, including halting US military aid to Israel and reforming campaign finance standards set by the Supreme Court case Citizens United.

“Unless Speaker Jeffries is willing to commit to enforcing our nation’s laws like the Leahy Law against Israeli genocide in Gaza, unless the speaker is willing to get to the heart of this crisis which is Citizens United, he will not have my vote,” the Ohio Democrat said in a video posted to social media.

Jeffries’s preemptive countermove effectively strips progressive members of leverage heading into Wednesday’s closed-door vote by forcing them to go on record against his leadership.

It also highlights a weakness in their efforts: the lack of another candidate for speaker.

On Monday, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts dismissed the idea she would mount a challenge to Jeffries.

Last week, she rallied her social media followers to sign a petition to shape the Democratic majority’s agenda, spurring questions about whether she would run for the speaker role. But she has since brushed those aside.

“I do not need to be the speaker of the House to speak for the people,” Pressley said at a town hall in her district.

When asked about the resistance he faces from his fellow Democrats, Jeffries told reporters they would “have to talk to” dissenting party members about why they oppose his leadership.

“We’re going to have a vote tomorrow. The caucus is going to be able to work its will. And we’ll see what the outcome is tomorrow,” Jeffries said. “In less than 24 hours, you’ll be able to know.”

Jeffries is expected to handily win Wednesday’s vote, which would give the leader an idea of the support he has when the 120th Congress is sworn in on January 3.

The speakership will be confirmed in a separate roll call vote on the floor of the US House early in the new year.

articles.title: Exclusive: Highly classified US national security communications network goes down, sources say
articles.summary: The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matte...
articles.body:
The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter.

The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said.

As the agency works to understand the scope of the problem, it has enacted staggered arrivals for personnel, the sources said.

"The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance," the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. "While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events."

A source familiar with the matter told CNN that restoration of the network was ongoing but not yet complete.

Earlier in the day, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said on Newsmax. "We see no evidence that this was a cyberattack. There is no crisis, or anything like that, for Americans to be worried about."

A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency's ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One.

Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

NSANet is "more of a network of networks, and it's unlikely that a full outage exists given the many redundancies in place," a former senior NSA official told CNN. "It could impact analysis and reporting, but for highest priority requirements they would find a way to work those. So it is alarming, but likely not crippling."

A voicemail inbox recording for NSA employees on Tuesday described the situation as a "code yellow," the second-highest in a three-level system that governs whether NSA employees report for work at the agency's Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters or not. The recording told non-emergency personnel to arrive for work in a staggered manner and for emergency personnel to arrive as usual. The New York Times first reported that detail.

The outage at America's most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country.

All flights nationwide were grounded for hours on Friday after a massive systems failure, leading to thousands of flights being delayed or canceled. The Federal Aviation Administration traced the problem to a single router in Arkansas.

Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Team meetings.

And in recent weeks banks and other services have experienced outages, on Monday thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts.

There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security.

The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official.

Tuesday's outage was not the first time the NSA's internal computer networks have suffered significant disruption. In 2000, a tech failure at the agency downed computers for nearly three days and interrupted the processing of intelligence at Fort Meade, an agency spokesperson said at the time.

This story has been updated with additional information.

CNN's Kylie Atwood and Haley Britzky contributed reporting.

articles.title: Dems campaign promise to freeze energy costs faces glaring reality check
articles.summary: Sam Romain of Americans for Energy Dominance says Democrats' energy price controls, from Gina Hinojosa's Texas rate freeze to state caps, can't fix supply.
articles.body: Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa is preparing her first step into left-leaning policies in the historically deep red state by implementing an emergency utility rate freeze — but one expert worries the proposal will become a failed attempt to address the affordability crisis. More Democratic-led states are looking to impose similar plans to Hinojosa's after she said on Day One of being governor that she will freeze residential electricity rates, an idea that many warn clashes with Texas’ uniquely competitive energy sector and could inadvertently create energy shortages. "It's a campaign promise they made on the trail," Sam Romain, chairman of the free market group Americans for Energy Dominance, told Fox News Digital. "But they don't have the power to just freeze the rates. You can't just wave a magic wand and freeze the rates." DEMOCRAT GINA HINOJOSA STUNS ABBOTT, MAKES HISTORY AS FIRST LATINA TEXAS GOVERNOR Romain believes it’s only a matter of time before Democrats across the country have to wrestle with ways to increase energy production — even as they are currently exploring a variety of energy price controls. "We know that price works based on supply and demand, right? It's basic, basic economics," Romain said. "And what you're seeing across the nation is this Democratic price control scheme that's dressed up as an emergency. The problem is you can't necessarily freeze your way out of the supply problems," Romain added. Some Democratic-led strategies aim to lock down energy prices while others look to subsidize them. Some plans call for both. In one such case, Democrat Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, who took office in January, is demanding a six-year rate freeze as a Florida company looks to buy Virginia’s largest energy supplier. She has also called for "a tripling of monthly bill credits for ratepayers." New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill promised to declare a state of emergency to cap energy rates at the outset of her term in January 2026, but has since pivoted to implement a credit system to offset electricity costs using executive orders. Among the newly elected Democrats, California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra promised to "institute a freeze on utility rates… while the state investigates long-term solutions to bring these costs under control," a strategy he framed as a priority. In Wisconsin, Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley will lead a legislature that last year entertained a proposal to cap gas and electricity bills at 4% of a qualifying household’s annual income. Crowley himself has also proposed a similar "fair deal" plan that would cap annual rent increases at 7%. DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT And in Ohio, Democratic state leadership led by House Minority Leader Dani Isaacsohn has proposed a 12-month freeze on utility rates as Amy Acton prepares to take the gubernatorial mansion. To Romain, these proposals deal a twofold blow. In addition to failing to build out supply, he believes they also discourage additional production. "A freeze in and of itself doesn't actually build anything. Actually, it does almost the opposite. It discourages developers from building. They don't know if they're going to be able to recoup their profit margin on their construction," Romain said. Questions also remain about the legality of some of the plans. In Texas, for instance, experts have noted that Hinojosa’s planned use of an emergency declaration may quickly run into legal resistance. Nick Loris, the president of C3 Solutions, a conservative coalition for climate solutions that focuses on energy, environment and agriculture policy, questioned the emergency powers Hinojosa says she plans to use. "The Texas Disaster Act lets the governor declare disasters and suspend the regulatory laws and statutes that are in existence. But I think there is a high degree of skepticism, both from courts, but also from state policymakers, that this warrants such a claim — and that it is such a disaster," Loris said. Romain believes Democrats will face similar legal hurdles in other states. But even though he expects price-control strategies to stall, Romain believes that creates an opportunity: fertile ground for a bipartisan affordability strategy as Democrats look to keep their commitments. "Democrats know there's a supply-side issue," Romain said. LIZ PEEK: DEMOCRATS’ AFFORDABILITY SCAM COLLAPSES IN STATES THEY ACTUALLY RUN "Their solution to it is different than the Republicans'… And the solution is quite simply to just let American companies build and compete. The problem is to unleash American innovation. This country was built by builders, right? And so let our companies build the tools they need, let them build the generation sites, let them build the power plants," Romain said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Permitting reform is one area in particular he believes may soon turn into an area for cooperation, a deregulation of the rules that govern energy production. "I'm actually really optimistic… that we're going to have a massive permit reform package done very quickly, very soon, actually," Romain said. "I think that we have a massive opportunity in front of us."

articles.title: Judge fires back at Fani Willis' office in courtroom clash over Trump case: 'Due process doesn't apply to you'
articles.summary: A Georgia appeals judge grilled Fani Willis' office over its bid to challenge nearly $17 million in legal-fee requests from Trump and other ex-defendants.
articles.body: A Georgia appellate judge pressed Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis’ office Tuesday as it pushed for permission to fight millions in legal-fee requests from President Donald Trump and other former defendants in her collapsed election interference case. Before a three-judge panel, Willis’ office argued it should be allowed to protect its budget from payments stemming from a prosecution she and her office were disqualified from handling in December 2024. "What process are you entitled to? You’re the government. Due process doesn’t apply to you," Judge J. Wade Padgett told Donald Wakeford, a chief senior assistant district attorney representing Willis’ office. Trump and other former defendants are seeking nearly $17 million under a Georgia law passed last year, with Trump alone requesting more than $6 million. The law allows defendants to recover legal fees if their prosecutor is removed for improper conduct and their charges are later dismissed. MIKE DAVIS: CALIFORNIA'S HIGHEST COURT DISGRACES ITSELF BY UPHOLDING DISBARMENT OF JOHN EASTMAN Tuesday’s hearing focused on whether Willis’ office could participate in challenging those requests. The state is represented in the reimbursement fight by Pete Skandalakis, executive director of the Prosecuting Attorneys’ Council of Georgia, who took over after Willis’ disqualification and moved to dismiss the charges in November 2025. Willis’ office argued he cannot adequately protect its financial interests because his own decision to drop the case opened the door to the reimbursement requests. Wakeford also argued that Skandalakis’ authority in the case ended when the prosecution did. "This statute has created a mess and that is no secret," Wakeford said of the new Georgia law allowing defendants to seek reimbursement for their legal fees. The judges pressed him on whether Willis’ disqualification still bars her office from participating. MIKE DAVIS: DISGRACED GEORGIA JUDGE MUST LEAVE THE BENCH OVER SEX SCANDAL "So let’s talk about the elephant in the room then," Padgett said, pointing to the court’s earlier ruling declaring the district attorney wholly disqualified. "The criminal prosecution has ended," Wakeford responded, arguing that the fee dispute is a separate matter. "Is the disqualification over? Is she no longer wholly disqualified?" Judge Ken Hodges asked. Wakeford said that Willis’ disqualification applied to the criminal prosecution, arguing it did not bar her office from participating in the separate legal-fee dispute. But the panel also questioned whether that finding satisfies the new law’s requirements for reimbursement. CALIFORNIA HIGH COURT ORDERS DISBARRING OF FORMER TRUMP ATTORNEY OVER EFFORT TO DISPUTE 2020 ELECTION RESULTS "The trial judge found an appearance of impropriety and found that actual misconduct had not been established," Padgett said. Willis and her office were removed from the case after an appeals court found that her romantic relationship with Nathan Wade, the special prosecutor she appointed, created an appearance of impropriety. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER In March, Fulton County Superior Court Judge Scott McAfee denied Willis’ request to intervene, finding that Skandalakis could adequately represent her office’s interests. Her office is asking the appeals court to overturn that decision. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The court announced no ruling during Tuesday’s hearing, leaving unresolved whether Willis’ office can directly challenge the fee requests.

articles.title: ‘Zero transparency’: Inside Trump’s plans for Venezuela’s oil money
articles.summary: Democrats say they plan to investigate Trump’s dealings with Venezuela after winning control of Congress.
articles.body:
The administration of United States President Donald Trump is facing criticism over how it has handled billions of dollars in oil revenue collected from Venezuela.

Since January 3, Trump’s government has controlled Venezuela’s oil exports, gathering the revenue in an account overseen exclusively by the US Treasury.

Last week, the Department of State released a 53-page report aimed at shedding light on the account’s activities. It revealed that at least $12.11bn have passed through the account since the start of the year.

But critics say the report lacks key details about where the money came from and who it is going to.

“There’s been zero transparency on all of the financial engineering associated with how $12bn of Venezuelan oil was changing hands and being utilised,” said Tyson Slocum, the director of the energy programme at Public Citizen, a US-based consumer advocacy nonprofit.

“All we have now is a very barebones narrative of how the funds were used, but not details on what entities were involved.”

Concerns about Trump’s plans for Venezuela’s oil sector began late last year, when his government began seizing oil tankers leaving the South American country.

Any oil on board, Trump said, would be kept or sold by the US. He and members of his administration framed the confiscated fuel as compensation for the losses incurred when Venezuela nationalised its oil industry decades ago.

“American sweat, ingenuity and toil created the oil industry in Venezuela,” White House aide Stephen Miller said at the time. “Its tyrannical expropriation was the largest recorded theft of American wealth and property.”

Tensions between the US and Venezuela reached a tipping point on January 3, when Trump authorised a military operation to abduct Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.

In a speech that morning, Trump highlighted the role oil had played in his decision. “We’re going to be taking out a tremendous amount of wealth out of the ground,” Trump said.

He proceeded to explain that some of the Venezuelan oil proceeds would go “to the United States of America in the form of reimbursement for the damages caused us by that country”.

Days later, Trump revealed he had spoken to oil companies “before and after” the operation. He also held a meeting with oil industry executives at the White House to discuss plans for Venezuela.

Legal experts have raised concerns that the January 3 operation was an attack on Venezuela’s sovereignty, in violation of international law.

They have also questioned the legality of seizing another country’s natural resources, given that a 1962 United Nations resolution grants nations “permanent sovereignty” over their own natural resources.

But supporters of Trump’s actions have pointed to Maduro’s history of violent repression and anti-democratic actions in Venezuela as justification for the operation.

Maduro has since been replaced by his former vice president, Delcy Rodriguez, who has largely cooperated with Trump’s demands.

But the focus on Venezuela’s oil revenue has left some critics questioning whether Trump plans to address the human rights issues in the South American country.

Trump has repeatedly downplayed the importance of democratic elections in Venezuela, said John Feeley, a former US ambassador and senior diplomat in Latin America.

“Trump has made patently clear that he has no interest in the democratic future of Venezuela,” said Feeley, calling the US-Venezuela relationship “protectorate neocolonialism”.

More recent manoeuvres have also raised speculation about the Trump administration’s commitment to transparency in its management of Venezuelan oil.

In late August, for instance, Trump announced his government would have a direct stake in extracting nearly a fifth of Venezuela’s oil.

Under the terms of the agreement, the US gained “majority control” in a 100-year deal for 17 Venezuelan oilfields, with proven reserves of 65 billion barrels.

North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), a company owned by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, was given the rights to operate the fields.

The Pentagon, meanwhile, took a 35 percent stake in the company, and the US was guaranteed 20 percent of the oil output at cost. Trump called it “the biggest oil deal in history”.

But Betancourt has faced investigations in the US, Spain and Switzerland over accusations of money laundering.

Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado also said the contract with NABEP “evidently does not reflect the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants”.

Venezuela has long struggled to export its oil, so the fact that it will now be sold on the open market is beneficial to the country’s economy, said Luis A Pacheco, a former executive with Venezuela’s state oil company and nonresident fellow at the Baker Institute Center for Energy Studies at Rice University.

But Pacheco is sceptical of Trump’s deal with NABEP.

“This is an obscure outfit with no known financial sources, with very little tech wherewithal,” he said. “This so-called mega-deal, without doubt, will certainly yield very little of what’s expected of it.”

Little transparency over billions of dollars

The shroud of secrecy surrounding the Venezuelan oil deals has spurred some Democrats in the US Congress to press for greater accountability.

In September, Democrats in the House of Representatives (PDF) and Senate asked the administration to disclose what had been uncovered by KPMG, an outside accounting firm hired to audit transactions involving Venezuelan oil exports.

The State Department did issue its report last week. But key portions were redacted, including who deposited money into the accounts and who the final recipients of the funds were.

Feeley, the diplomat, said there are also questions about the total sum of the proceeds. Only $12bn is accounted for in the report.

“We have no idea how that money was used, and we have no idea what percent of the total amount of money deposited in the US Treasury that $12bn represents,” said Feeley. “But most experts allege that it is only a fraction.”

In a statement to Al Jazeera, a State Department spokesperson said its report “provides a comprehensive account, down to the cent, of the Venezuelan natural resource revenues deposited in, held by, and disbursed” from the account.

Venezuela’s requests for disbursement are checked against a “list of approved and prohibited expenditure categories”, the spokesperson added.

The funds are then used for “essential public services, macroeconomic stability, and the rebuilding of key sectors such as energy, healthcare and infrastructure”.

But who receives those funds remains unclear. Pacheco said there is no reason the US could not disclose details of the monetary flow.

“Even though this report gives you some information, it still doesn’t give you light into the most important thing, which is what is the Venezuelan regime is doing with the money,” Pacheco said.

“You can affirm with very good certainty, when you talk about billions of dollars, something is draining away.”

Pacheco also questioned the supervisory role the Trump administration has claimed over the Venezuelan government. At one point, Trump even claimed he would “run” the South American country.

“The discourse of the White House is that they exert some sort of tutelage over the Venezuelan regime,” Pacheco said. “But apparently that tutelage doesn’t go as far as to tell the Venezuelans where is the money going to.”

But this year’s midterm elections could usher in a wave of oversight into the Venezuelan oil money.

Democrats won majority control in both the House and Senate in the November 3 midterm elections, and lawmakers have already floated the possibility of opening investigations, once the new Congress arrives in January.

“The admin is sending billions to Delcy Rodriguez’s corrupt government where the list of who benefits is kept murky,” Representative Joaquin Castro wrote on social media after the election.

“I will continue to demand answers, and use every tool we will have with the incoming Democratic majority, including congressional hearings, to uncover what the United States is doing in Venezuela.”

One area of exploration might be the role private oil trading companies play in the Trump administration’s deal. Firms like Vitol, a Dutch multinational energy company, could be put under the microscope.

A week before Trump sent troops into Caracas to abduct Maduro, John Addison, a senior trader with Vitol, held a secret meeting with Vice President JD Vance on a tarmac in Montana, according to the news agency Reuters.

Vitol was later able to buy oil from the state-owned Venezuelan oil company at a steep discount. Addison and his wife donated $6m to Trump’s election campaign in 2024.

Democrats on the House Oversight Committee have long been eager to investigate the dealings of firms like Vitol in Venezuela.

“Oversight Democrats will not stop until we know exactly what companies are profiting from these foreign policy decisions, especially in Venezuela,” Representative Robert Garcia said in January .

Garcia is expected to chair the oversight committee next year.

articles.title: AOC, Paris Hilton, Florida Rep Lee 'hopeful' law against sexually explicit deepfakes can pass
articles.summary: Paris Hilton discusses the shame she carried after her leaked early-2000s sex tape as she pushes the DEFIANCE Act to protect deepfake victims.
articles.body: Entrepreneur Paris Hilton brought to light her experience being victim to sexual exploitation on "America Reports" as she advocated alongside Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Laurel Lee, R-Fla., to pass legislation protecting victims of digital sexual abuse and deepfake pornography. Hilton has lobbied extensively for the DEFIANCE Act, which would allow victims of nonconsensual, AI-generated sexual deepfakes to sue the creators or distributors. "Back when I was 19, and this happened to me, there were no laws to protect me," Hilton told Fox News in reference to her leaked sex tape in the early 2000s. "The laws need to catch up with this technology," she added. CHRIS HANSEN URGES PARENTS TO TEACH CHILDREN ABOUT ONLINE PREDATORS BEFORE ALLOWING INTERNET ACCESS A victim of deepfakes herself, Hilton is back in Washington, D.C., continuing her advocacy and opened up about how that and her leaked early-2000s sex tape affected her. "It was humiliating and I felt so much shame for so many years when that shame should never have been on myself, and it just breaks my heart thinking of all these young girls, and they don't have the team or resources to help them," she said. Ocasio-Cortez is also a victim of sexually explicit deepfake images and said victims deserve to have the right to hold their perpetrators accountable in court. BIPARTISAN LAWMAKERS WANT TO STRIP BIG TECH'S LEGAL IMMUNITY THAT CAN SHIELD SOCIAL MEDIA COMPANIES "This is a form of digital sexual abuse that people deserve to be protected on, and also, victims deserve to have the right of action to go after predators in court," Ocasio-Cortez said. The Democratic congresswoman noted how easy it is for users to create deepfake images given advancements of artificial intelligence chatbots, and Hilton explained how innocent images can be manipulated for dark purposes. SHE DIDN’T EXIST, BUT THE MONEY DID: A REAL INFLUENCER SOUNDS THE ALARM ON AI DECEPTION "Due to the explosion in chatbots, it's now easier than ever to generate these kinds of images," Ocasio-Cortez said. "You don't need to know Photoshop, you don't need to have any sort of special skills, and so, the instances of this kind of abuse has just utterly exploded." "With this technology, you don't even have to know the person. They could just take an innocent yearbook picture, a family photo, and turn it into something that's sexually explicit," Hilton said. The Senate already passed the DEFIANCE Act, but the House has not moved much on the legislation since being re-introduced in May 2025, despite having bipartisan support. House members must greenlight it by Jan. 3 to avoid having to restart the legislative process. "But guardrails are not enough. We need law, and we need it signed into law," Ocasio-Cortez said. HOUSE BACKS MASSIE'S PUSH TO RELEASE TAXPAYER-FUNDED SEXUAL HARASSMENT SETTLEMENT RECORDS Lee said the DEFIANCE Act is an example of what legislators can "do right" in Washington, D.C. "As technology continues to advance, we have to think about our laws and think about the ways that predators are behaving to be sure that we're keeping up. We've seen too many examples already of this happening to people in America, and this is a great step forward to shutting it down," Lee said. CONVICTED PREDATORS FACE LIFETIME BARRIER UNDER GOP LAWMAKER’S SWEEPING VICTIM PROTECTION BILL Ocasio-Cortez and Lee agreed that passing the DEFIANCE Act in the House would set the tone for bipartisanship as Democrats prepare to take congressional majorities in January. "We have an opportunity to come together and prioritize the things that bring us together instead of prioritizing the things that split us apart," Ocasio-Cortez told Fox News. "I am so encouraged by the level of bipartisan support for getting this across the finish line, and I have every confidence that either in this Congress or early in the next, we're going to be able to get it done," Lee said. "It’s just very scary that this is legal, and there should be no question about it," she said. "This should be passed."

articles.title: POWs, teens among 6 US soldiers from Korean War identified seven decades later
articles.summary: The DPAA identified six U.S. soldiers missing from the Korean War, including two teenagers, decades after they died as prisoners of war or in action.
articles.body: At least six U.S. soldiers who went missing during the Korean War, including two teenagers, have been identified decades after their deaths. The soldiers, who ranged in age from 18 to 28, all served in the U.S. Army, the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA) said. Five were junior enlisted soldiers or noncommissioned officers, including four corporals and one sergeant. The sixth was a commissioned officer, a first lieutenant. Officials said the soldiers either died as prisoners of war or were presumed killed in action. The soldiers identified were Cpl. Jackie Lee Thurman, 18, of Illinois; 1st Lt. Raymond Banker Gilbert, 23, of Ohio; Cpl. Richard Neal Lennox, 18, of Michigan; Cpl. William Reynold Laughlin Jr., 21, of Oregon; Sgt. Joseph Alfred Platzkoester, 28, of Illinois; and Cpl. Andrew R. Tischler, 21, of Celina, Texas. EXPERTS FINALLY SOLVE MYSTERY OF TEENAGE REVOLUTIONARY WAR SOLDIER 246 YEARS AFTER HIS DEATH Most of the soldiers had been buried for decades as "Unknowns" at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific, also known as the Punchbowl, in Honolulu, Hawaii. Their remains were later disinterred through DPAA initiatives between 2016 and 2024 and sent to the agency's laboratory for modern forensic analysis. Gilbert, a member of Battery B, 503rd Field Artillery Battalion, 2nd Infantry Division, was wounded and captured before being reported missing on Dec. 1, 1950. He died from his wounds as a prisoner of war on Jan. 31, 1951. His remains were returned in 1954 and buried as an Unknown in Honolulu. They were disinterred in July 2024, and he was officially identified on June 4, 2026. ‘FREEDOMS ARE NEVER FREE’: A JEWISH AMERICAN SOLDIER BURIED WITH NAZIS FINALLY LAID TO REST WITH US TROOPS Thurman, a member of Battery B, 99th Field Artillery Battalion, 1st Cavalry Division, went missing on Sept. 3, 1950, while attempting to escort a wounded officer under heavy mortar fire near Taegu and Waegwan, South Korea. His remains were eventually recovered in 1952 and buried as an Unknown in Honolulu. They were disinterred in November 2022, and he was officially identified on May 18, 2026. Lennox, a member of Company C, 1st Battalion, 7th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, was reported missing on Nov. 28, 1950, following an enemy attack near Sachang-ni, North Korea. He was captured and taken to Prisoner of War Camp 1 in Changsong, where he died nearly a year later in October 1951. His remains were returned in 1954 and buried as an Unknown in Honolulu. They remained there until they were disinterred on June 13, 2016. He was officially identified on Aug. 7, 2025. Laughlin Jr., a member of Company D, 1st Battalion, 32nd Infantry Regiment, 7th Infantry Division, went missing on Dec. 2, 1950, during a withdrawal near the Chosin Reservoir. He was never reported as a prisoner of war, and the Army issued a presumptive finding of death on Dec. 31, 1953. His remains were returned in 1954 and buried as an Unknown in Honolulu. They were disinterred in July 2022, and he was officially identified on Sept. 28, 2026. Platzkoester, a member of Company H, 2nd Battalion, 38th Infantry Regiment, 2nd Infantry Division, went missing on May 30, 1951, during a convoy ambush near Inje, South Korea. The Army issued a presumptive finding of death in December 1953 and declared his remains unrecoverable in January 1956. Unbeknownst to officials at the time, his remains had already been recovered in the fall of 1951 and later buried as an Unknown in Honolulu in 1956. They were disinterred in November 2023, and he was officially identified on May 29, 2026. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Tischler, a member of Company F, 2nd Battalion, 15th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, was reported missing in action on May 25, 1951, during a road march near Taewol Village, South Korea. The DPAA officially accounted for him on May 5, 2026. Each soldier is memorialized on both the Courts of the Missing in Honolulu and the Korean War Veterans Memorial Wall in Washington, D.C.
